extracted.intended_audience: business leaders, managers, industrialists, and aspiring entrepreneurs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical management, hiring, organizational, and personal-guidance principles for running industrial enterprises, public speaking, and authorship as illustrated by Carnegie's experience at mills and in public life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote those who render exceptional service
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no way of making a business successful that can vie with the policy of promoting those who render exceptional service."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote from within individuals who demonstrate exceptional zeal, knowledge, and industry (examples: William Borntraeger, William L. Abbott, Mr. Curry). Promotions may include partnership interests; such promotions reward merit and drive business success. Example: the poor German lad rose from clerk to partner and later received a deserved income of about $50,000 a year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single command in a works (no dual authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Upon no account could two men be in the same works with equal authority. An army with two commanders-in-chief... could not fare more disastrously than a manufacturing concern with two men in command upon the same ground."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign clear, sole responsibility for a works or plant to a single manager who reports to higher management. Avoid splitting equal authority between two supervisors in the same physical operations; Carnegie credits this decision (making Mr. Jones 'captain') with major success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit-for-role: do not expect office men to succeed in manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: "It was unjust to expect him, or any other office man, to be able to step into manufacturing and be successful from the start. He had neither the knowledge nor the training for this new work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate candidates by relevant domain skills. A person excellent in one function (e.g., auditing/accounts) may not be suitable for hands-on manufacturing leadership. Place people in roles that match training and experience; retraining may be required before a role change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Own raw materials and finish the completed article
rubrics_metrics.description: "The one vital lesson in iron and steel that I learned in Britain was the necessity for owning raw materials and finishing the completed article ready for its purpose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue vertical integration when supply uncertainty/higher costs threaten production: build or acquire upstream capacity (e.g., blast furnaces) and finish products ready for market (example: producing spiegel and ferro-manganese domestically to replace costly foreign imports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purchases of inferior plants
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing so unsatisfactory as purchases of inferior plants."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious buying second-hand or inferior production plants—costs may equal new construction yet deliver inferior performance. (Example: the reconstructed Escanaba furnace cost as much as a new one and never was as good.) Note: an initially poor purchase can sometimes yield unexpected later uses, but it is a risky, generally undesirable choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate accounts and clerks checking transfers are highly profitable
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is nothing more profitable than clerks to check up each transfer of material from one department to another in process of manufacture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement rigorous accounting and internal controls to track costs and inter-department transfers; precise accounts enable knowledge of exact profit margins and better management decisions. This administrative investment pays dividends in profitability and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make granted partnership interests payable only from profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnership interests given to employees or collaborators were structured "to be paid only from future profits" and "we always provided that the cost of the interest given was payable only out of profits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When granting equity/interests to key employees, structure the financial obligation so the firm bears the cost only from realized profits, limiting immediate capital requirements and financial exposure. This can encourage acceptance and align incentives without imposing cash burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire and promote internal staff who show zeal, curiosity, and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: William Borntraeger came as a non-English-speaking minor employee, learned quickly, 'was everywhere about the mill, knowing everything, and attending to everything' and rose to partnership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and cultivate employees who demonstrate unflagging zeal, industry, willingness to learn, and active engagement with operations. Such traits indicate high promotability; invest in and reward them (travel, promotion, partnership) as productive long-term assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select leaders for practical competence over external reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Competence in manufacturing may not correlate with reputation in other fields (example: a railway auditor with deserved reputation in accounts failed in manufacturing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appointing plant or operational heads, prioritize demonstrable practical manufacturing or operational skill rather than solely relying on reputations from other sectors. Use hands-on evidence and trial observation when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public speaking rule: be natural and speak to people as people
rubrics_metrics.description: "When you stand up before an audience reflect that there are before you only men and women. You should speak to them as you speak to other men and women in daily intercourse... Be your own natural self... 'Avoid elocutionists like snakes,' he said, 'and be yourself.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For effective oratory, address audiences conversationally and honestly; avoid affected elocution or trying to be someone else. Practitioners (example: advice from Colonel Ingersoll) attribute power to authenticity rather than theatrical artifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing advice: write for friends; sincerity and ease produce merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'writer of a book designed for his friends' should 'just say what you really feel.' Carnegie notes that books written without effort and without trying to make an impression often succeed, and he wrote for friends rather than fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing narratives or essays, aim for honest expression targeted to a sympathetic audience; contrivance to impress is likely counterproductive. Authentic, effortless-seeming writing often resonates better with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel widely to broaden intellectual outlook and synthesize ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie: 'Every person who can, even at a sacrifice, make the voyage around the world should do so.' Travel led him to study Confucius, Buddha, Zoroaster and to synthesize a broader philosophical view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extended travel and exposure to diverse cultures and texts to achieve intellectual integration, comparative understanding of religions/philosophies, and refreshed perspective—valuable for leaders and thinkers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal compatibility test for choosing a life partner
rubrics_metrics.description: Carnegie applied a personal test (quoting Ferdinand in The Tempest) to determine his wife's suitability: she alone passed his 'supreme test' among many acquaintances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend applying deep, candid personal criteria (values, character, capacity to be 'helpmeet') rather than superficial considerations. Carnegie suggests an introspective test of fit before committing to marriage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensate key managers in the form they prefer to avoid distraction
rubrics_metrics.description: When offered partnership (equity) the Captain declined: 'I don't want to have my thoughts running on business. I have enough trouble looking after these works. Just give me a h--l of a salary if you think I'm worth it.' Carnegie replied: 'All right... the salary of the President of the United States is yours.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor compensation to the preferences and priorities of key operational leaders—some prefer high salary and focus on management rather than equity. Respecting such preferences preserves focus and prevents management distraction.
